newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: US demands bigger Western say in African Bank.
newsitem.headline: US demands bigger Western say in African Bank.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday made a strong bid for Western state shareholders to have more say in the affairs of the African Development Bank, setting the scene for a fight with Nigeria which is opposed to change.
Currently African states hold two-thirds of the shares in the AfDB, with Western governments holding the rest.
The Bank's management wants a capital increase by 1999, but the Western governments -- which would have to find the money -- will only agree if their voting power is increased.
"Our hopes for the negotiations are simple," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told the first day of the Bank's three-day annual meeting here.

"Through a limited capital increase we seek a non-regional (non-African) capital share of 45 percent and Executive Board voting rules that will ensure us a more effective voice in the institution," he added.
However, Nigeria, the Bank's single biggest shareholder with 10 percent of the capital, has ruled out any dilution of the African vote.

Finance Minister Anthony Ani told Emerging Markets newspaper this week: "I have made it clear that Nigeria opposes any increase in the non-regional 33-1/3 percent stake in the Bank and that remains our position."

The Bank's management hopes the board will agree to a capital increase at the 1998 annual meeting, but the dispute threatens a rerun of the row that closed the Bank's soft-loan arm for almost two years until May 1996.
Western shareholders refused to replenish the African Development Fund until a new management team reformed the Bank's operations.
Summers told a news conference that new voting arrangements should ensure big decisions could not be taken without the support of the non-African shareholders.
"I think it will be very unfortunate if the opposition continues because the opportunity to further restore the credibility of the Bank with its supporters and the markets will be lost," he said.
AfDB President Omar Kabbaj has introduced stricter lending criteria and tighter recruitment procedures to turn the Bank around, to the applause of most of the shareholders.

However, it still has an arrears problem, and Ivory Coast finance minister N'Goran Niamien warned against complacency. "These payment delays continue to represent a serious threat to our institution as regards its financial situation," he said.
Niamien noted that the bulk of the arrears was owed by countries going through periods of political or social crisis.

At the end of 1996, Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo, had arrears of 329 million units of account, or $474 million, representing around 57 percent of the total arrears of some $829 million.
The Bank's annual report said Angola, Congo, Liberia and, to a lesser extent, Somalia also had significant arrears.
AfDB president Omar Kabbaj admitted progress had been "mixed" on the arrears question, but he said outstanding arrears had declined by nine percent by the middle of April this year.
